keyTerms.definition: One nested layer of the ladder. Shells 0-1 live in items 1-2, shells 2-3 in items 3-6.

recall.question: How do shells map to items, and what checks the depth gate?
recall.answer: Shells 0-1 live in items 1-2, shells 2-3 in items 3-6, shell 4 in item 7, shell 5 in item 8, shell 6 in item 9, shell 7 in item 11, shell 8 in item 10, shell 9 in item 12, shell 10 in item 13(c). Item 13 checks the depth gate.

keyTerms.definition: Adapting the base model: new context length, knowledge cutoff, or domains. Different objective, data, and evals from pretraining.
A binary switch per token. SFT sets 1 on assistant tokens the model should learn to generate.
Low-rank adaptation. It freezes W and learns a low-rank delta BA: cheap to store and swap, limited in expressivity.
Concatenating short sequences into full bins with attention masked at boundaries, so no padding is paid for.
New gradients overwriting old knowledge. It is measured on base evals, not assumed.
The protocol both sides speak. Train on A and serve with B, and the model reads roles as gibberish.

recall.question: What are the three training stages and how do they differ?
recall.answer: Pretraining builds the base. Midtraining adapts it: context length, cutoff, domains. Post-training teaches behavior with SFT and RL. Each has its own objective, data, and evals.

recall.question: Why is SFT data quality more critical than pretraining data quality?
recall.answer: SFT data is small and precious; each example is seen many times. One bad example repeated 100x is 100 bad lessons.

recall.question: What does the tool result count as during SFT, and why?
recall.answer: Environment observation, like a user message. The model reads it but must not learn to emit it; the call itself is the taught behavior.
